p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Not long ago, millets such as ragi, jowar and bajra were dismissed in many Indian cities as the food of the poor, to be replaced by polished rice and refined wheat as soon as a family could afford them. The change was understandable. White rice and soft wheat bread were quicker to cook, easier to digest for those unused to coarse grains, and carried the prestige of prosperity. Government procurement and distribution, which favoured rice and wheat for decades, reinforced the shift, and in many regions farmers turned land once sown with millets to more profitable crops.

Opinion has since begun to turn. Millets are now praised for their fibre and minerals, and for the modest demands they make on the farmer: many grow on poor soils with little water and tolerate heat that would wither other cereals. Recipes once kept by grandmothers are reappearing in restaurants and packaged foods. The revival is welcome, but it carries a certain irony. A grain that was abandoned because it signalled poverty is being rediscovered partly because it now signals discernment, and the price of some millet products in city shops would surprise the farmers who grow them. If the revival is to last, it will need to reach ordinary kitchens and fields, and not remain a fashion for those who can afford to follow fashions.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Fish in the open sea belong to no one until they are caught, and this simple fact lies at the heart of many fisheries' troubles. A fisherman who leaves young fish in the water so that they may grow and breed cannot be sure that he will be the one to benefit; a rival boat may simply catch them the next day. Each crew therefore has reason to take as much as it can, even when all of them can see that the stock is shrinking. Economists call such situations a tragedy of the commons, and the open ocean is perhaps its most familiar example.

The tragedy is not inevitable. Coastal communities in many parts of the world have long maintained customary rules: seasons when fishing stops, areas closed to nets, limits on the mesh size that lets small fish escape. The annual pause during the monsoon on India's western coast, when many fish breed, rests on a similar idea, though it is now enforced by law rather than by custom alone. Such rules work best when those who must obey them have had a hand in making them and can see that others are obeying too. Where enforcement is weak, or large trawlers from outside ignore the restrictions that local boats observe, trust collapses and the old race to the last fish resumes.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Cooking Techniques for Coarse Grains
The Return of the Humble Grain
Why Rice Is Healthier Than Millets
The Failure of Government Procurement
questions.why: Main idea: millets, once dismissed, are being revived.

questions.q: According to the passage, white rice and wheat replaced millets partly because they:
opts: Were cheaper than millets in every region.
Were quicker to cook and carried the prestige of prosperity.
Contained more fibre and minerals.
Grew on poorer soils with less water.
questions.why: Detail: they 'were quicker to cook, easier to digest... and carried the prestige of prosperity'.

questions.q: The "irony" mentioned in the passage is that:
opts: Grandmothers refuse to share their recipes.
Millets grow well only where water is plentiful.
Farmers now earn more from millets than anyone else.
A grain once rejected as a sign of poverty is now valued as a sign of refined taste.
questions.why: Inference: 'abandoned because it signalled poverty... rediscovered partly because it now signals discernment'.

questions.q: The author's chief concern about the millet revival is that it:
opts: May remain limited to affluent consumers instead of reaching ordinary households and farmers.
Is based on false claims about nutrition.
Will force farmers to stop growing millets.
Will make rice and wheat disappear entirely.
questions.why: Attitude: it must 'reach ordinary kitchens and fields, and not remain a fashion for those who can afford to follow fashions'.

opts: Carelessness
Refined judgement
Hunger
Poverty
questions.why: Vocabulary: millets now signal good taste, the opposite of their earlier association with poverty.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: The Life Cycle of Ocean Fish
Why the Monsoon Ruins Fishing
The Commons at Sea and the Rules That Protect It
The Economics of Trawler Manufacture
questions.why: Main idea: the open sea is a commons, but shared rules can prevent its tragedy.

questions.q: According to the passage, the monsoon pause on India's western coast is based on the fact that:
opts: Fish move to deeper water in the monsoon.
Fish prices fall sharply during the rains.
Many fish breed during that season.
Boats cannot be repaired during the rains.
questions.why: Detail: 'The annual pause during the monsoon on India's western coast, when many fish breed'.

questions.q: Which situation would the author most likely see as another example of a 'tragedy of the commons'?
opts: Villagers each grazing extra cattle on a shared pasture until the grass is exhausted.
A farmer overworking his own private field.
A cooperative fixing milk prices by a fat test.
A government selling a forest to a company.
questions.why: Inference: the tragedy arises when no one owns a shared resource, so each user takes as much as he can despite visible decline.

questions.q: The author mentions customary rules mainly to show that:
opts: Fishing should be banned throughout the year.
Coastal communities are hostile to outsiders.
The tragedy of the commons can be avoided through shared restraint.
Custom is always stronger than law.
questions.why: Purpose: they follow 'The tragedy is not inevitable'.

opts: Unforgivable
Invisible
Unavoidable
Intended
questions.why: Vocabulary: the tragedy is not certain to happen, as customary rules show.
